Antithrombotics

Recall
Reversal: UFH vs LMWH vs warfarin?
tap to flip
Answer
UFH → protamine sulfate (cationic binding neutralizes heparin).
LMWH → protamine, partial reversal.
Warfarin → vitamin K + 4-factor PCC; plasma only if PCC is unavailable (ACC 2020). PCC replaces factors II, VII, IX, X at once; vitamin K restores their hepatic synthesis.
🩺 Think it through
STEMI is diagnosed, but PCI cannot be delivered promptly. What is the life-saving strategy?
LIFE-SAVING = reperfusion: PCI is preferred; give fibrinolysis if appropriate when PCI cannot be delivered promptly.
Recall
ACS antiplatelet therapy — FIRST-LINE single and dual?
tap to flip
Answer
FIRST-LINE antiplatelet: aspirin.
FIRST-LINE dual therapy: aspirin + P2Y12 inhibitor.
Recall
Acute anticoagulation in ACS?
tap to flip
Answer
UFH/LMWH as clinically indicated
Board trap · Nitrates in MINitroglycerin is the anti-ischemic only if the patient is not hypotensive/preload dependent. AVOID nitrates in hypotension, preload-dependent RV infarction, recent PDE5 inhibitor.
Recall
Secondary prevention after MI?
tap to flip
Answer
High-intensity atorvastatin/rosuvastatin; β-blocker when indicated; ACEi/ARB especially with LV dysfunction/DM/HTN
Board trap · Fibrinolysis outside STEMIAVOID fibrinolysis in NSTEMI/unstable angina.
Board trap · PrasugrelAVOID prasugrel with prior stroke/TIA.
Board trap · β-blocker in acute MIUse β-blocker cautiously in shock, severe bradycardia, acute HF, high-grade block.
  • ★Monitoring in ACS: ECG/ST changes; troponin; hemoglobin/platelets; renal function for anticoagulants; aPTT/anti-Xa with UFH as appropriate; LDL response after high-intensity statin.

🔴Cellulitis & Cutaneous Abscess17 items▾

Recall
Cellulitis — what is it, and which organisms are classic?
tap to flip
Answer
Spreading infection of the dermis/subcutaneous tissue; classically β-hemolytic streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus. The antibacterial must achieve active concentrations in the infected soft tissue.
Recall
How do β-lactams kill streptococci/MSSA, and what is their killing pattern?
tap to flip
Answer
Bind penicillin-binding proteins → inhibit transpeptidation/peptidoglycan cross-linking. Killing is principally time-dependent (as with vancomycin) — unlike the concentration-dependent aminoglycosides/fluoroquinolones.
Recall
Why do ordinary β-lactams fail against MRSA, and why does vancomycin still work?
tap to flip
Answer
MRSA commonly expresses an altered PBP. Vancomycin bypasses PBPs and interferes directly with cell-wall precursor processing — a bactericidal cell-wall inhibitor, renally eliminated, and the classic standard parenteral drug for methicillin-resistant staphylococci.
Skin and soft-tissue antibacterials — core drugs
ClassPrototype / alternativesMOAKey PK / PDMajor ADRsBoard role / cautionsAnswer
First-generation cephalosporin (β-lactam)Cephalexin, cefazolinPBP inhibition → ↓cell-wall cross-linking → bactericidal cell-wall failureCephalexin PO; cefazolin IV; largely renalAllergy, GI, rare C. difficileStreptococci/MSSA. Caution: severe β-lactam allergy; renal adjustment
Penicillinase-resistant penicillinDicloxacillin, nafcillin/oxacillinPBP inhibitionDicloxacillin PO; nafcillin/oxacillin parenteral; hepatic handling important for nafcillinAllergy, hepatic/renal effects—
GlycopeptideVancomycinBinds D-Ala-D-Ala → inhibits cell-wall synthesis/transglycosylationIV for systemic infection; renal eliminationNephrotoxicity, infusion-related histamine reactionMRSA killing / severe Gram-positive infection. Renal dosing/exposure

Recall
Nonpurulent cellulitis vs abscess at the bedside?
tap to flip
Answer
Nonpurulent cellulitis: diffuse erythema, warmth, edema and tenderness without a discrete fluctuant collection.
Abscess: fluctuance, focal tenderness, purulent drainage — bedside ultrasound may identify an occult collection when the examination is equivocal.
  • ★Skin-infection pathway: diffuse nonpurulent cellulitis, stable → FIRST-LINE streptococcal/MSSA-active β-lactam (cephalexin or dicloxacillin) → fluctuant purulent collection → I&D (drain the focus) first → severe systemic disease/MRSA risk → MRSA-active systemic therapy, classically IV vancomycin for severe disease → no improvement → reassess drainage, necrosis, resistant organism or alternative diagnosis.
Recall
Which features increase the need for systemic MRSA-active therapy?
tap to flip
Answer
Purulence (it changes MRSA probability; nonpurulent → think streptococci/MSSA), systemic illness, immunocompromise, recurrent infection, rapid spread, or severe local disease/severe cellulitis and other high-risk features.
Board trap · Antibiotics alone for a drainable abscessA cutaneous abscess is a high-inoculum purulent cavity: incision and drainage corrects the key mechanical lesion and is pharmacologically more important than simply escalating systemic antibiotics. CONTRAINDICATED strategy: antibiotic-only management of a large, accessible fluctuant abscess when drainage is required. Fluctuant abscess → think drainage before adding more antibiotic.
Board trap · “Just cellulitis” with red flagsRapid progression, bullae, crepitus, skin necrosis, hypotension, severe pain out of proportion or systemic toxicity → evaluate for necrotizing soft-tissue infection, not simple cellulitis.
Recall
When is culture actually useful in skin infection?
tap to flip
Answer
From purulent drainage, severe disease, recurrent infection or unusual exposures. Uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis often has no useful culture target.
Recall
What to review before choosing a skin-infection antibiotic?
tap to flip
Answer
Renal function, β-lactam allergy, previous MRSA, recent antimicrobial therapy, pregnancy and immune status.
Board trap · Oral MRSA drug = streptococcal drug?Doxycycline/TMP-SMX are common oral MRSA options, but do not reflexively assume they give equally reliable streptococcal coverage in every cellulitis scenario.
Recall
Vancomycin — what to monitor and why?
tap to flip
Answer
Adjust exposure to kidney function; monitor creatinine and therapeutic exposure in prolonged/severe infection — accumulation increases nephrotoxicity. Vancomycin + other nephrotoxins → additive renal injury → AKI.
  • ✎Doxycycline absorption is reduced by chelation with ; it is generally avoided in when safer alternatives exist.
Recall
TMP-SMX + ACE inhibitor/ARB/MRA (K⁺-retaining drugs) or renal dysfunction → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Additive K⁺ retention → important hyperkalemia; monitor K⁺ and creatinine in high-risk patients.
Recall
Persistent fever or spreading erythema despite apparently active therapy → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Reassess for undrained abscess, necrotizing infection, resistant pathogen, osteomyelitis or incorrect diagnosis — not blind antibiotic escalation.

💀Drug-Induced Cutaneous Disorders: Anaphylaxis & SJS/TEN18 items▾

Recall
Mechanism of immediate drug hypersensitivity?
tap to flip
Answer
IgE-mediated type I: mast-cell degranulation → histamine/leukotriene release → vasodilation, vascular leak and bronchoconstriction.
Recall
Mechanism of delayed drug eruptions and SJS/TEN?
tap to flip
Answer
Frequently T-cell–mediated; SJS/TEN = severe cytotoxic epidermal injury with widespread keratinocyte apoptosis.
Recall
Classic drug culprits for severe cutaneous reactions?
tap to flip
Answer
Sulfonamides (skin rash, exfoliative dermatitis and rare but potentially fatal Stevens–Johnson syndrome), aromatic antiseizure agents, allopurinol, selected NSAIDs and several antimicrobials.
Recall
Sulfonamides — toxicities beyond the skin?
tap to flip
Answer
Hematologic toxicity, crystalluria and G6PD-associated hemolysis, complicating severe cutaneous reactions.
  • ✎Severe-cutaneous-reaction pharmacogenomic pairings in susceptible populations: carbamazepine–HLA-B and allopurinol–HLA-B.
Recall
Simple exanthematous drug eruption — appearance?
tap to flip
Answer
Symmetric morbilliform/maculopapular rash without extensive mucosal injury or skin detachment.
Recall
Which findings mark immediate hypersensitivity, and which define anaphylaxis?
tap to flip
Answer
Urticaria, angioedema, wheeze, hypotension or airway compromise = immediate hypersensitivity; hypotension/bronchospasm/angioedema = anaphylaxis.
Recall
Airway compromise / hypotension / bronchospasm after a drug → ?
tap to flip
Answer
LIFE-SAVING IM epinephrine immediately — the first-line drug of choice for anaphylaxis/immediate anaphylactic shock. Monitor airway, BP, HR, O₂ saturation.
🧠 Memory toolEpinephrine in anaphylaxis — receptor by receptor
α1Vasoconstriction: raises SVR, decreases mucosal edema
β1Cardiac support: increases cardiac output
β2Bronchodilates and reduces mediator release
Sympathomimetic; given IM.
Board trap · Antihistamine or steroid for anaphylaxisCONTRAINDICATED: treating anaphylaxis with antihistamine alone — a wrong board answer; delayed epinephrine can be fatal. Antihistamines and steroids act more slowly, are less effective and are adjuncts only. Never substitute antihistamine or steroid for epinephrine.
Recall
H1 antihistamines and glucocorticoids in acute drug hypersensitivity — what does each do, and what can neither do?
tap to flip
Answer
H1 antihistamine (diphenhydramine/cetirizine): competitive/inverse H1-receptor antagonism reduces urticaria and pruritus (urticaria only, stable → H1 antihistamine for symptoms) but does not reverse shock or life-threatening airway obstruction.
Glucocorticoid (methylprednisolone/prednisone): intracellular GR activation alters inflammatory transcription; onset is delayed, so it is adjunctive — not an epinephrine substitute.
  • ✎Classification by epidermal detachment: SJS body-surface area, SJS/TEN overlap , TEN .
Recall
SJS/TEN warning features?
tap to flip
Answer
Fever, painful dusky or targetoid skin, mucosal erosions, blistering, positive epidermal detachment and systemic involvement.
  • ★Continuing antigenic drug exposure is the initiating lesion of a severe drug reaction, so the single most important first pharmacologic action is immediate withdrawal of the culprit agent (mandatory). Painful drug rash + mucosal erosions + blistering → treat as SJS/TEN: stop the culprit immediately → burn/ICU-level (critical) supportive care → fluid/electrolyte replacement, wound care, pain control, temperature control and ophthalmologic/mucosal management.
Recall
Is there an antidote for SJS/TEN?
tap to flip
Answer
No single universal antidote — management is stopping the antigenic drug + supportive care. Cyclosporine, systemic glucocorticoids, etanercept or IVIG have been used in selected settings, but none is established as a universally proven antidote or standard pharmacologic rescue regimen.
Board trap · Rechallenge after SJS/TENCONTRAINDICATED: rechallenge with the culprit drug after SJS/TEN except under extraordinary specialist circumstances; recurrence may be rapid and severe.
Recall
Working up a suspected drug rash — what gives the diagnosis?
tap to flip
Answer
Review all recently introduced drugs and stop nonessential high-risk medications; the correct pharmacologic diagnosis often depends more on temporal exposure than on serum drug levels.
Recall
Monitoring in SJS/TEN?
tap to flip
Answer
Skin-detachment extent (BSA), fluids, electrolytes, renal/hepatic (organ) function, infection and ocular/genitourinary mucosal complications.

🤕Pain Management: NSAIDs, Acetaminophen & Opioids22 items▾

Arachidonic acid cascade — where each anti-inflammatory acts
StepBlocked byAnswer
Membrane phospholipids → arachidonic acid (phospholipase A2)Corticosteroids (inhibit phospholipase A2)
COX pathway → prostaglandin/thromboxane precursorsNSAIDs block COX: aspirin/nonselective NSAIDs reduce both COX-1 and COX-2 products; celecoxib preferentially inhibits COX-2
LOX pathway → leukotrienesMontelukast blocks the CysLT1 receptor (the receptor for LTD4) — a leukotriene-receptor antagonist acting downstream; it does not inhibit the LOX enzyme

  • ★Drug map: anti-inflammatory/pain drugs branch into aspirin/nonselective NSAIDs, COX-2 inhibitors and acetaminophen; RA therapy branches into conventional/biologic DMARDs; gout divides into acute anti-inflammatory drugs and chronic urate-lowering drugs.
  • ★Lesion-first approach: identify whether the lesion is infection, immune inflammation, degeneration, nociceptive signaling, bone resorption or crystal deposition → select the drug whose molecular target corrects that lesion → predict its mechanism-based toxicity and required monitoring.
Recall
How do NSAIDs relieve inflammatory pain?
tap to flip
Answer
Prostaglandins sensitize peripheral pain fibers and amplify inflammatory nociception; NSAIDs inhibit COX → ↓prostaglandins → analgesic + antipyretic + anti-inflammatory effects.
Recall
What is unique about aspirin among NSAIDs?
tap to flip
Answer
Aspirin irreversibly inhibits COX; most other NSAIDs are reversible inhibitors.

Board trap · COX-2 selective = safe?Celecoxib lowers COX-2 inflammatory prostaglandins while relatively sparing platelet COX-1 — as selectivity shifts from nonselective toward COX-2, platelet/GI COX-1 inhibition decreases. COX-2 selectivity is not cardiovascular safety.
  • ★NSAID dose-response: increasing COX inhibition improves inflammatory pain until an analgesic ceiling is approached; further dose escalation disproportionately increases GI, renal and BP toxicity rather than giving unlimited analgesia.

Recall
Acetaminophen overdose — mechanism of liver injury and the antidote?
tap to flip
Answer
Well absorbed orally, hepatically metabolized, t½ 2–3 h. Normal doses are cleared mainly by conjugation; overdose saturates the safe pathways → progressively more toxic P450-derived metabolite until glutathione is depleted → hepatic necrosis.
N-acetylcysteine restores sulfhydryl/glutathione capacity and detoxifies the toxic metabolite — potentially lifesaving, most effective when given early.
Board trap · Waiting for symptoms after acetaminophen overdoseThe patient may be initially asymptomatic and look well. Use serum concentration/timing + early NAC — do not delay NAC until clinical liver failure develops. Monitor acetaminophen level, AST/ALT, INR.
Recall
μ-Opioid receptor signalling — how is pain transmission reduced?
tap to flip
Answer
Couples to Gi/o → ↓adenylyl cyclase/cAMP, opens postsynaptic K⁺ channels and closes presynaptic Ca²⁺ channels → reduced neurotransmitter release and pain transmission.
  • ★Opioid dose-response: increasing μ-receptor occupancy increases analgesia but also progressively increases respiratory depression, sedation and constipation; high-efficacy full agonists have no reliable respiratory “ceiling”.
🧠 Memory toolOpioid overdose — the triad
1CNS depression
2Respiratory depression (bradypnea)
3Miosis (pinpoint pupils)
Opioid-treated patient with pinpoint pupils + bradypnea → naloxone and airway support.
Recall
LIFE-SAVING management of opioid overdose?
tap to flip
Answer
Airway/ventilatory support + naloxone. Naloxone is a competitive antagonist: it shifts opioid agonist signalling downward/rightward only while present; as its concentration falls, a longer-lasting opioid reoccupies receptors → recurrent toxicity, so repeat dosing may be needed when the opioid outlasts the antagonist. Monitor RR, consciousness and recurrence.
Recall
Neuropathic pain — which drugs fit the mechanism?
tap to flip
Answer
α2δ calcium-channel ligands (gabapentin/pregabalin — need renal dose adjustment), SNRIs or selected TCAs — may respond better than escalating NSAIDs or opioids.
  • ★Choosing by pain type: mild–moderate inflammatory pain → NSAID if renal/GI/CV risk acceptable (normal kidney/GI status makes it logical; severe CKD/GI bleed changes the drug choice) → noninflammatory pain/high NSAID risk → acetaminophen where appropriate → severe acute pain → multimodal therapy ± opioid with respiratory monitoring → neuropathic pain → gabapentinoid/SNRI/TCA approach.
Recall
How should pain be classified before choosing a drug target?
tap to flip
Answer
Inflammatory, mechanical, neuropathic, visceral, acute postoperative/traumatic, malignant or chronic.
Board trap · Sedation mistaken for successPain relief should come with improved function; progressive sedation is toxicity, not therapeutic success.

Loss of bone strength from imbalance between osteoclast-mediated resorption and osteoblast-mediated formation.

How should oral alendronate be taken?

Fasting, with plain water; remain upright afterward to limit esophageal injury; avoid simultaneous calcium/iron/food.

Recall
Estrogen/SERMs vs chronic glucocorticoids — effect on bone?
tap to flip
Answer
Estrogen/SERM effects decrease postmenopausal resorption. Chronic systemic glucocorticoids do the opposite (reduce bone maintenance) and are a major pharmacologic cause of osteoporosis.
  • ★Treatment ladder: always correct significant hypocalcemia/vitamin-D deficiency first → fragility fracture/high fracture risk → antiresorptive therapy if no contraindication → suitable for oral therapy → FIRST-LINE common antiresorptive: oral alendronate or another bisphosphonate → PREFERRED alternatives: GI/adherence issue → IV zoledronate (IV bisphosphonate) or denosumab when clinically appropriate → very high fracture risk → anabolic strategy with teriparatide.
  • ★Calcium/vitamin-D adequacy should accompany osteoporosis pharmacotherapy unless contraindicated.
Board trap · Antiresorptive in the wrong patientCONTRAINDICATED: untreated hypocalcemia before bisphosphonate/denosumab; significant esophageal disease or inability to remain upright for oral bisphosphonates. Osteoporosis + esophageal disease → avoid the oral bisphosphonate; consider a nonoral strategy.
Board trap · Stopping denosumab abruptlyDenosumab should not be abruptly discontinued without transition therapy — rebound bone resorption can precipitate vertebral fractures.
Recall
Who should not receive teriparatide?
tap to flip
Answer
Patients at increased baseline osteosarcoma risk: open epiphyses (children/young adults), Paget disease or other metabolic bone disease besides osteoporosis, bone metastases or prior skeletal malignancy, prior skeletal radiation, hereditary predisposition to osteosarcoma (FDA label 2020).
The boxed osteosarcoma warning was removed in 2020; use beyond 2 years in a lifetime is considered only if fracture risk remains or has returned to high.
Classic textbook: boxed osteosarcoma warning with a strict 2-year lifetime limit.
Recall
Severe renal dysfunction — effect on osteoporosis drug choice?
tap to flip
Answer
Changes bisphosphonate choice/dosing and increases hypocalcemia risk with denosumab.
Recall
Osteoporosis — what to assess before treatment?
tap to flip
Answer
Fragility-fracture history, DEXA bone-mineral density, age, menopause/hypogonadism, chronic glucocorticoid use, falls, calcium/vitamin-D intake and renal function.
Recall
Osteoporosis therapy — what to monitor, and how is success measured?
tap to flip
Answer
Monitor Ca²⁺, vitamin D, renal function, dental risk, BMD and interval fragility fractures. Success = fracture prevention, BMD trajectory, adherence and minimal therapy-specific toxicity.

Autoimmune inflammatory synovitis involving T cells, B cells, macrophages and cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6, with progressive cartilage/bone destruction.

Symmetric inflammatory polyarthritis, prolonged morning stiffness, synovial swelling and progressive deformity.

Reduces immune-cell/inflammatory activity; the classic anchor conventional DMARD and FIRST-LINE disease-modifying anchor when appropriate. Start low-dose methotrexate relatively early in moderate–severe RA to reduce disease progression.

Recall
Which drugs raise methotrexate toxicity?
tap to flip
Answer
Probenecid (blocks tubular secretion of weak-acid drugs — methotrexate is the classic example) or an NSAID in high methotrexate exposure → ↓renal elimination → ↑MTX toxicity.
Recall
What do biologics/targeted therapies do that analgesics do not?
tap to flip
Answer
Interrupt specific pathways — TNF, IL-6, B cells, T-cell costimulation, JAK signaling — rather than giving nonspecific symptomatic analgesia.
  • ★RA treatment ladder: confirmed active RA → initiate disease-modifying therapy early → methotrexate suitable → anchor DMARD → NSAIDs and short-course glucocorticoids = symptom control/bridge only, not definitive structural treatment and never a replacement for a DMARD in progressive RA → persistent disease/failure of adequate conventional therapy → combination csDMARD or biologic/targeted therapy → before biologic/JAK therapy → infection + latent-TB screening.
Recall
Before major immunosuppression or anti-TNF therapy in RA — what must be checked?
tap to flip
Answer
Latent TB, hepatitis risk, vaccinations and active infection. TNF inhibitors and other biologics can reactivate latent infection: screen for TB and avoid starting a biologic during serious active infection.
🩺 Think it through
An RA patient has good pain relief on an NSAID, but radiographs show progressive erosions. What changes?
Add/escalate a DMARD — not simply more NSAID. NSAIDs reduce prostaglandin-mediated pain and stiffness but do not modify the underlying immune disease or prevent erosions/structural damage; DMARDs are defined by their ability to slow (slow disease modification) or sometimes reverse joint damage — methotrexate/DMARD does, NSAID does not. Treatment is adjusted whenever clinical/radiographic progression continues despite apparent symptom control.
Recall
RA assessment — what to evaluate?
tap to flip
Answer
Inflammatory activity, functional impairment, erosions, RF/anti-CCP, CBC, renal/hepatic function and extra-articular disease.
Recall
What must be distinguished from active RA before escalating immunosuppression?
tap to flip
Answer
Septic arthritis, gout, OA and fibromyalgia.
Recall
Hydroxychloroquine and chronic glucocorticoids — long-term safety points?
tap to flip
Answer
Hydroxychloroquine: dose/risk-based retinal (ophthalmologic) monitoring, by cumulative exposure. Chronic glucocorticoid exposure adds osteoporosis, diabetes, cataract and infection risk.

Primarily degenerative articular cartilage loss with subchondral remodeling and variable secondary synovial inflammation.

Improved pain and function — not suppression of inflammatory biomarkers.

🦠Septic Arthritis11 items▾

Recall
Septic arthritis — why is it a joint emergency?
tap to flip
Answer
Bacterial infection of the synovial space: bacterial proliferation plus neutrophilic inflammation can rapidly destroy cartilage; delayed antimicrobial/drainage therapy can result in irreversible joint destruction.
Recall
Septic arthritis — organisms?
tap to flip
Answer
S. aureus is a major pathogen; Gram-negative bacilli and N. gonorrhoeae become important according to age and exposure.
Recall
Acute monoarthritis with pain, warmth, marked limitation of motion and fever → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Treat as septic arthritis until excluded.
  • ★LIFE-SAVING diagnostic step: arthrocentesis — cell count, Gram stain, culture and crystals — before antibiotics when feasible without dangerous delay. Obtain blood cultures in febrile/systemically ill patients.
Board trap · “Crystals, so it is gout”CONTRAINDICATED strategy: diagnosing an acute hot monoarthritis as gout without synovial evaluation when septic arthritis is plausible. Aspirate before calling it gout — urate crystals do not reliably exclude simultaneous infection; do not assume gout merely because crystals are present.

DrugClass / MOAPKRoleToxicityAnswer

Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Antimicrobials kill organisms; joint drainage reduces pus, bacterial inoculum and destructive inflammatory pressure. Septic arthritis = antimicrobial therapy + drainage of the infected focus.
Recall
Which settings change the likely organism and regimen in septic arthritis?

Prosthetic joint, recent surgery, injection-drug use, gonococcal exposure and immunosuppression.
Recall
Septic joint not improving despite susceptible antibiotics → think?

Inadequate drainage, osteomyelitis, prosthetic infection, abscess or incorrect diagnosis.
Recall
Septic arthritis — monitoring?
tap to flip

Fever, pain/range of motion, cultures, inflammatory-marker trend, CBC, renal/hepatic toxicity and adequacy of drainage.

Recall
Why does TB arthritis demand combination therapy?
tap to flip
Answer
An indolent osteoarticular infection by slow-growing intracellular mycobacteria — slow growth, intracellular location, chronicity and resistance; monotherapy rapidly selects resistant organisms. Multidrug therapy attacks extracellular and intracellular organisms in different metabolic compartments while preventing/delaying resistant mutants.
Board trap · Single-drug treatment of active TBCONTRAINDICATED: monotherapy for active osteoarticular TB — never treat active disease with single-drug INH.

Mycobacterial culture/NAAT and often synovial tissue/biopsy — not ordinary bacterial culture alone.

Other pulmonary/extrapulmonary TB sites and HIV/immunosuppression; baseline hepatic and renal function plus visual acuity/color discrimination; a complete medication review, because rifampin profoundly alters CYP/P-gp substrate exposure.

Oral contraceptives, warfarin, azoles, antiretrovirals and many others — enzyme/transporter (CYP/P-gp) induction → ↓drug efficacy.

Monosodium urate crystal deposition secondary to chronic hyperuricemia; crystals activate synoviocytes, macrophages and neutrophils → intense neutrophilic inflammation.

Abrupt severe monoarthritis, classically the first MTP joint, with redness, swelling and exquisite tenderness.

Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent monosodium urate crystals in synovial fluid.

How do chronic urate-lowering drugs help?
tap to flip

They reduce urate production or increase excretion → prevent new crystal deposition and gradually dissolve existing stores.
Recall

tap to flip
Answer
Allopurinol, started low and titrated to a serum-urate target — for recurrent/high-burden gout.
Recall
Why can starting urate-lowering therapy trigger flares, and what prevents them?
tap to flip
Answer
Effective allopurinol/febuxostat progressively lowers serum urate, but early mobilization of tissue urate may transiently increase flare frequency before the crystal burden declines → temporary anti-inflammatory flare prophylaxis with low-dose colchicine/NSAID where appropriate.
Recall
Probenecid — transport mechanism and the low-dose paradox?
tap to flip
Answer
Competes for proximal-tubular weak-acid transport → ↑urate excretion; at low doses, competing effects on secretion can paradoxically raise serum urate. It also raises levels of other weak-acid drugs by blocking tubular secretion.
Board trap · Allopurinol/febuxostat + azathioprine or 6-MPMajor, dangerous interaction: xanthine oxidase contributes to thiopurine elimination, so XO inhibition raises thiopurine exposure dangerously → severe marrow/thiopurine toxicity.
Board trap · Colchicine overdoseSevere diarrhea is common at high doses; overdose can be fatal with multiorgan, marrow, hepatic and renal toxicity. There is no routine universal antidote — intensive supportive/toxicology care (support organ failure); monitor CBC, renal, hepatic, ECG.
Recall
Colchicine + strong CYP3A4/P-gp inhibitor → ?
tap to flip
Answer
↓Clearance → markedly raised colchicine exposure → potentially fatal colchicine toxicity; risk especially high with renal/hepatic impairment.
Recall
IL-1 inhibitors in gout — place?
tap to flip

Selected refractory/contraindicated cases only; not the classic PLE prototype.
Recall
What to determine before choosing acute/chronic gout therapy?

Renal function, ulcer/CV risk, interacting drugs and urate burden.
Recall
Monitoring on urate-lowering therapy?

Answer
Serum urate, renal/hepatic function, rash, flare frequency and adherence. SJS/TEN-like rash on allopurinol → immediate drug discontinuation.

🦋Systemic Lupus Erythematosus & Connective-Tissue Autoimmunity9 items▾

Recall
SLE — immunopathology?
tap to flip
Answer
Systemic autoimmune disease with B-cell autoantibody production, immune complexes, T-cell abnormalities and inflammatory organ injury.
Recall
What decides how intensely SLE is immunosuppressed?
tap to flip
Answer
Organ involvement. Skin/joints alone (mild cutaneous/musculoskeletal disease) need less immunosuppression than nephritis, CNS disease, pulmonary hemorrhage or severe vasculitis — determine whether kidney, CNS, blood, lung or cardiovascular systems are involved.
SLE immunomodulators (belimumab is the agent listed specifically for SLE; hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, cyclosporine and rituximab are among the other immune-modifying agents)
DrugMOARoleToxicityAnswer
HydroxychloroquineModifies lysosomal antigen processing/TLR signaling → reduces chronic autoimmune activationGenerally a maintenance cornerstone for many SLE phenotypesRetinopathy
Glucocorticoid — prednisone/methylprednisoloneIntracellular GR activation → altered inflammatory gene transcription (rapid, broad suppression)Rapid efficacyDose-dependent infection, osteoporosis, diabetes, cataract, myopathy and HPA suppression
Mycophenolate mofetilConverted to mycophenolic acid → inhibits IMPDH → preferentially suppresses lymphocyte guanine synthesisAntimetabolite: steroid-sparing control in organ-threatening diseaseGI effects, marrow suppression, infection, teratogenicity
CyclophosphamideAlkylating agent producing phosphoramide mustard and acroleinSevere organ-threatening autoimmune diseaseMarrow suppression, infertility, malignancy, hemorrhagic cystitis
AzathioprineConverted to 6-mercaptopurine → purine-synthesis inhibitionAntimetabolite: steroid-sparing control in organ-threatening diseaseMarrow toxicity — affected by TPMT/NUDT15 status
BelimumabInhibits B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS)SLENausea, diarrhea, respiratory infection
Recall
Cyclophosphamide bladder toxicity — cause and prevention?
tap to flip
Answer
Acrolein → hemorrhagic cystitis → MESNA + hydration (MESNA binds urinary acrolein). Monitor urinalysis, hematuria.
🧠 Memory toolPregnancy and immunosuppressants — stop vs continue
STOP — contraindicatedMethotrexate, mycophenolate
CONTINUE when appropriateHydroxychloroquine is commonly continued in pregnancy
Recall
Before major immunosuppression in SLE — baseline checks?
tap to flip
Answer
CBC, renal/hepatic function, urinalysis/proteinuria assessment, pregnancy status, infection screening and vaccination review.
Board trap · Flare or infection?Infection can mimic a lupus flare — escalating immunosuppression before excluding infection can be dangerous. SLE/psoriasis immunosuppression should not be escalated blindly.
Recall
What usually sets treatment intensity in lupus nephritis?
tap to flip
Answer
Renal biopsy.
Recall
SLE monitoring?
tap to flip
Answer
Disease-specific organs plus CBC, LFTs, creatinine, urinalysis/proteinuria, retinal health and infection. Follow both inflammatory disease activity and irreversible organ damage — do not treat a laboratory value in isolation.

🩹Psoriasis & Psoriatic Arthritis11 items▾

Recall
Psoriasis — pathophysiology?
tap to flip
Answer
Principally an immune-mediated dermatologic disease (grouped with the connective-tissue diseases): pathologic T-cell/cytokine signaling with accelerated keratinocyte proliferation and inflammatory plaque formation; systemic joint disease = psoriatic arthritis.
Recall
Where can psoriasis drugs act?
tap to flip
Answer
Locally on epidermal proliferation/inflammation, or systemically on T cells and cytokines such as TNF, IL-12/23, IL-17 and IL-23. Methotrexate/cyclosporine broadly suppress immune proliferation; biologics interrupt specific cytokine pathways.
Recall
Plaque psoriasis — appearance?
tap to flip
Answer
Sharply demarcated erythematous plaques with scale, commonly on extensor surfaces/scalp.
Recall
Which questions identify psoriatic arthritis?
tap to flip
Answer
Inflammatory back pain, swollen joints, dactylitis and enthesitis.
Board trap · Analgesics alone in psoriatic arthritisPain-only treatment does not alter destructive psoriatic arthritis — disease-modifying therapy is required when inflammatory joint disease is present.
Recall
Topical or systemic therapy — what decides?
tap to flip
Answer
Body-surface involvement, special-site involvement, quality-of-life effect and joint disease.
Psoriasis therapies
DrugMOAUseToxicity / monitoringAnswer
Topical corticosteroidGR agonism suppresses local inflammatory transcriptionTopicalProlonged/high-potency use: skin atrophy, telangiectasia; systemic HPA suppression when large areas are treated
Vitamin-D analog — calcipotrieneVDR activation normalizes keratinocyte differentiation/proliferationTopicalHypercalcemia is uncommon at standard topical exposure
MethotrexateCytotoxic/immune-modifying DMARDSystemic, for severe skin disease or psoriatic arthritisMonitor marrow, liver and pregnancy risk: contraindicated in pregnancy; CBC/LFT/creatinine monitoring
CyclosporineCalcineurin inhibition → ↓IL-2/T-cell activationRapid systemic efficacyNephrotoxicity and hypertension restrict long-term use (monitor BP)
TNF inhibitors — infliximab/adalimumab/etanerceptNeutralize TNF signalingInflammatory diseaseSerious infection/TB reactivation: do not start in uncontrolled serious infection; latent-TB screening required
IL-17/IL-23 pathway biologicsHighly targeted cytokine-pathway blockadeModern options for plaque psoriasis/psoriatic arthritisInfection and agent-specific immune effects require monitoring
Recall
Before systemic immunosuppression/biologics in psoriasis — what to evaluate?
tap to flip
Answer
CBC/LFT/renal function, TB/hepatitis risk and active infection. Pregnancy, liver disease, renal disease and infection status substantially modify systemic-drug selection.
Board trap · Systemic steroids for psoriasisChronic systemic glucocorticoid monotherapy is generally undesirable in psoriasis — toxicity and risk of disease rebound.
Recall
Cyclosporine + nephrotoxic drugs or strong CYP3A4 inhibitors → ?
tap to flip
Answer
Markedly increased renal/systemic toxicity.
Recall
Psoriasis — monitoring on systemic therapy?
tap to flip
Answer
Skin/joint response, CBC, LFTs, renal function, BP with cyclosporine, and biologic-specific infection risks.
